Learning Objectives
Understand options for the nonsurgical management of cavovarus foot deformity, including
physical therapy; pharmacologic management; and orthotics, braces, and shoes.
Introduction
A cavovarus deformity is a common foot deformity with several possible etiologies. It is
characterized by hindfoot varus and an elevated medial longitudinal arch. Many patients are
afforded substantial relief with nonsurgical treatment.

Management: Goals of management are to reduce pain and allow patients to ambulate with a
stable foot and ankle.
Indications

Indications
The nonsurgical management of cavovarus deformity should be a multidisciplinary
approach involving physiatrists, physical therapists, orthotists, and pedorthists. The goal
of management is to maximize patient mobility and function, reduce pain, and allow the
patient to ambulate with a stable foot and ankle. Although nonsurgical management
cannot correct deformity or prevent deformity progression, physical therapy, bracing,
orthotics, and shoe modifications may afford symptomatic relief and improved
function.1,2 Response to nonsurgical management usually is best early in the disease
process in patients in whom the deformity is flexible or relatively mild.3
Contraindications

Contraindications
In patients with active infection or pending skin breakdown, urgent surgical treatment
may preclude the nonsurgical management of an advanced cavovarus deformity.
Techniques/Procedures
Physical therapy
Eversion and dorsiflexion stretching
Quadriceps strengthening
No benefit from plantar fascial stretching
Pharmacologic management

Techniques/Procedures
Physical therapy may provide benefit in patients in the early stages of progressive
deformity with a still-supple foot. A stretching and strengthening program incorporating
eversion and dorsiflexion of the foot and ankle with quadriceps strengthening may help
control pain and maximize function.1,3 Although recommended in the past, no evidence
demonstrates a benefit from plantar fascial stretching.1

The goal of pharmacologic management via drugs, such as baclofen, diazepam, and
dantrolene, is to manage spasticity in patients with a neuromuscular cavus foot.4
Intramuscular injections of botulinum toxin A have been beneficial in managing
spasticity and improving gait kinematics and plantar foot pressure distribution in
patients with cerebral palsy and stroke4-6 (Resource 1).
The appropriate orthotic for a cavovarus foot incorporates accommodative, shock-
absorbing materials with a total contact design to distribute pressure from bony
prominences and attenuate shock on rigid joints. A lowered arch; recessed first
metatarsal head; lateral forefoot wedge; and elevated, cushioned heel should be
incorporated to manage the elevated arch, plantar-flexed first metatarsal, forefoot
valgus, heel varus, and equinus deformities, respectively1,3,7-12 (Figures 1 and 2; Table
1; and Resources 2 and 3). Orthopaedic surgeons are obligated to examine the orthotic
given to a patient with a cavovarus foot. Often, such an orthotic has an elevated medial
arch and is rigid, accentuating the deformity and creating additional disability. The
orthotist may attempt to match the elevated arch with such a device, creating increased
difficulty for the patient. Instructions to the orthotist are the obligation of the
orthopaedic surgeon, and the orthotic should be assessed after construction and use.
Figure 1 Photograph shows a subtle cavus foot orthosis with a recessed first metatarsal
head, low medial arch, and lateral hindfoot wedge. (Reproduced with permission from
Chilvers M, Manoli A II: The subtle cavus foot and association with ankle instability and
lateral foot overload. Foot Ankle Clin N Am 2008;13[2]:315-324.)

Figure 2 Illustrations show posting of foot deformities. A, Medial (MED) forefoot posting
of a pes planus deformity accommodates forefoot varus (dorsiflexed first ray), which is
driving the hindfoot into valgus. B, Lateral (LAT) forefoot posting of a cavus deformity
accommodates forefoot valgus (plantarflexed first ray), which is driving the hindfoot into
varus. (Reproduced from Doty JF, Coughlin MJ: Shoes and orthoses, in Chou LB, ed:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2014, pp 13-23.)
Table 1 Ankle-Foot Orthosis Types and Modifications
Solid-ankle AFO
Trimlines fully enclose the malleoli to substantially
decrease mobilization of the foot and ankle complex
Semisolid-ankle AFO
Trimlines enclose the posterior soft tissues but do not
project anteriorly along the malleoli; allows limited ankle
motion with weight bearing but dampens ground
reaction forces
Posterior leaf spring AFO
Trimlines generally are narrow posteriorly and flexible
enough to allow normal weight-bearing motion; retains
enough shape memory to assist in foot dorsiflexion
during the swing-through phase
Articulated AFO
Separate foot and leg segments are connected by an
articulating mechanism aligned with the axis of the ankle
to allow controlled dorsiflexion and plantar flexion. The

hinge mechanism can be adjusted or modified to restrict
or assist in certain motions.
Wrap-around AFO
Completely encloses the foot, ankle, and lower leg;
maximizes skin contact area and may more effectively
maintain desired alignment
Double upright AFO
Often attaches to the exterior of the shoes; skin contact is
avoided, which may be more desirable for patients with
varied amounts of swelling or skin breakdown
Carbon fiber AFO
Incorporates many of the same designs and functions of
plastic AFOs; the carbon allows the orthosis to be less
bulky and provides energy storage in recoil, which
returns force to the patient during gait
Post
Wedge under the medial or lateral forefoot used to bring
the floor up to a fixed varus or valgus deformity or used
in the hindfoot medially or laterally to tilt the heel
Cutout
Cutout, well, recess, or depression that can be used in
the forefoot, midfoot, or hindfoot to unload a specific
area
Lift
Generally used as a neutral heel wedge to generate
equinus and relax the Achilles tendon
Cushion
Foam or other soft material used plantarly in the
forefoot, midfoot, or hindfoot to relieve plantar pressure
at painful areas
Extension
Rigid extension to the tips of the toes to decrease
bending forces of the midfoot and forefoot
Flange
Semirigid rim or lip extension on the orthosis to help
support or build up a certain area such as a collapsed
arch
Metatarsal bar
Pad placed proximal to the metatarsal heads to unload
plantar pressure at the area distal to the pad
AFO = ankle-foot orthosis.

Shoe modifications may include extra depth and width to fit insertable orthoses, relieve
impingement on claw toes, a high instep, or adducted forefoot.1,8-10,12 Lateral flare on
the sole of a shoe widens the base of support and decreases inversion episodes in
patients with lateral ankle instability8-10,12 (Figure 3;Resources 4 and 5).
Figure 3 Photographs (A and B) show shoe modifications. Modifications may include
extra depth and width to fit insertable orthoses, relieve impingement on claw toes, a
high instep, or adducted forefoot. Lateral flare on the sole of shoes widen the base of
support and decrease inversion episodes in patients with lateral ankle instability.
(Reproduced with permission from Jannisse DJ: Pes cavus foot: It isn’t really that hard to
manage. Why, what and how. Presented at the Orthopedic Foot Club Meeting, Brooklyn,
NY, December 6-7, 2019.)
Patients with ankle instability also may benefit from use of a high-top boot, off-the-shelf
ankle brace, or Arizona brace.3,11,12 Patients with severe ankle or subtalar instability,
severe muscle weakness, or rigid deformity require a custom-molded AFO.3,4,8,11,12
Integration of orthotic modifications into the foot bed of an AFO provides improved
proprioception and ankle stability.3,12 Incorporating a hinge with dorsiflexion assist
allows for a more normal gait pattern with use of an AFO.3,8 In patients with severe
equinus deformity, a clamshell design may be required to maintain control of the
deformity3,12 (Figure 4; Resource 6).
